q: Which amino acid has a nonpolar side chain?
h: Look for a side chain made only of carbon and hydrogen.
w: Valine's side chain is an isopropyl group, a hydrocarbon, so valine is nonpolar. Serine is polar neutral (O), lysine is basic (N) and aspartic acid is acidic.

q: At its isoelectric point (pI), an amino acid exists mainly as
c: a zwitterion with a net charge of zero
a cation with a net charge of +1
an anion with a net charge of −1
h: The pI is the pH where positive and negative charges balance.
w: At the pI the amino acid is H3N+–CHR–COO−, a zwitterion with zero net charge, so it does not move in an electric field.

q: Glycine (pI ≈ 6.0) is placed in a solution at pH 1. Which form is present mainly?
h: At a pH far below the pI, extra H<sup>+</sup> is available. Which group picks it up?
w: At low pH the –COO− is protonated, giving H3N+CH2COOH with a net +1 charge. The zwitterion is the form at pH 6; H2NCH2COO− is the high-pH form.

q: A peptide bond is formed between
c: the –COOH of one amino acid and the –NH<sub>2</sub> of the next
the side chains of two neighboring amino acids
the –NH<sub>2</sub> groups of two neighboring amino acids
the –COOH groups of two neighboring amino acids
h: A peptide bond is an amide bond, and water is released when it forms.
w: The carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of the next form an amide, –CO–NH–, releasing H2O. Side chains are not involved.

q: What is the name of the tripeptide Ala–Gly–Ser (written from the N-terminal end)?
h: Every residue except the C-terminal one gets the ending “-yl.”
w: Start at the N-terminus: alanyl, glycyl, then the C-terminal residue keeps its full name: alanylglycylserine. Reversing the order names a different peptide.

q: How many peptide bonds are in a tetrapeptide?
h: Each bond connects two neighboring amino acids in a chain.
w: Four amino acids in a row are joined by 3 peptide bonds (n − 1).

q: In sickle-cell anemia, glutamic acid at position 6 of the hemoglobin β chain is replaced by valine. Which level of protein structure is changed directly?
h: Which level of structure is defined by the amino acid sequence?
w: Changing one amino acid changes the sequence, the primary structure. The new nonpolar valine then makes hemoglobin molecules clump, affecting higher levels as a consequence.

q: The α helix and the β-pleated sheet are stabilized mainly by
c: hydrogen bonds between backbone C=O and N–H groups
disulfide bonds between cysteine side chains
salt bridges between acidic and basic side chains
h: Secondary structure involves only the repeating backbone atoms, not the R groups.
w: In secondary structure, the C=O of one peptide bond hydrogen bonds to the N–H of another. Disulfides and salt bridges involve side chains and belong to tertiary structure.

q: A disulfide bond between two cysteine side chains in the same polypeptide chain stabilizes which level of protein structure?
h: Interactions between side chains that fold a single chain into its 3-D shape belong to which level?
w: Side-chain interactions within one chain (disulfides, salt bridges, H bonds, hydrophobic attractions) make up tertiary structure. Quaternary would require bonds between separate chains.

q: Hemoglobin is made of four polypeptide subunits (two α and two β) held together. This describes its
h: Which level applies only to proteins with more than one polypeptide chain?
w: The arrangement of multiple subunits in one active protein is quaternary structure. Each subunit has its own primary through tertiary structure.

q: A 70% isopropyl alcohol swab disinfects skin before an injection by denaturing bacterial proteins. Denaturation disrupts
c: secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure, but not peptide bonds
only the peptide bonds that join the amino acids together
the primary structure, but no higher levels of structure
all levels, breaking the protein into free amino acids
h: Denaturation unfolds a protein. Does it break covalent peptide bonds?
w: Denaturing agents (heat, alcohol, acids, heavy-metal ions) break the interactions that fold the protein but leave the peptide bonds intact, so the primary structure survives. Breaking peptide bonds is hydrolysis.

q: Which process breaks a protein's primary structure, as happens during digestion?
h: Primary structure is held together by covalent amide bonds. What reaction breaks an amide?
w: Digestive enzymes (or strong acid with heat) carry out hydrolysis, adding water across peptide bonds to free amino acids. Heat and pH changes only denature.

q: In a globular protein dissolved in water, which side chain is most likely buried in the interior of the folded protein?
h: Polar and charged side chains like water. Where do nonpolar ones go?
w: Hydrophobic interactions pull nonpolar side chains such as leucine's isobutyl group into the interior, away from water. Charged lysine and glutamate and polar serine stay on the surface.

q: In phenylketonuria (PKU), the enzyme that converts phenylalanine to tyrosine is missing. Which statement about a person with PKU is correct?
c: Tyrosine becomes essential, and phenylalanine intake must be limited
Phenylalanine becomes nonessential, so it can be eaten freely
Tyrosine builds up to toxic levels, so it must be avoided
Aspartame is safe because it contains no amino acids at all
h: If the conversion step is blocked, which amino acid piles up, and which one can no longer be made in the body?
w: Phenylalanine (and phenylpyruvate) builds up and can damage the developing brain, so its intake is limited. Because the body can no longer make tyrosine from phenylalanine, tyrosine must come from the diet. Aspartame contains phenylalanine, which is why diet drinks carry a PKU warning.

q: Which amino acid is essential for adults and must be obtained from the diet?
h: Nonessential amino acids can be made in the body, often by transamination of keto acids from glycolysis or the citric acid cycle.
w: Lysine is essential (along with His, Ile, Leu, Met, Phe, Thr, Trp and Val). Alanine, glutamate and serine are made from pyruvate, α-ketoglutarate and a glycolysis intermediate. Corn is low in lysine, so corn-based diets need complementary proteins.

q: Collagen is a triple helix. In scurvy, a lack of vitamin C weakens collagen because vitamin C is needed to
c: hydroxylate proline and lysine so the strands can hydrogen bond
form the peptide bonds between glycine and proline in each chain
make disulfide bonds that hold the three strands together
attach glucose units that make the collagen water soluble
h: Hydroxyproline and hydroxylysine carry extra –OH groups. What attraction can –OH groups form between strands?
w: Vitamin C is required by the enzymes that convert proline and lysine into hydroxyproline and hydroxylysine, whose –OH groups hydrogen bond and hold the triple helix together. Without it, collagen is weak, causing bleeding gums and poor wound healing.

q: Which protein is correctly matched with its function?
c: collagen: carries oxygen in the blood
h: Recall the protein classes: transport, storage, structural, hormone, enzyme, protection and contractile.
w: Myoglobin stores O2 in muscle. Hemoglobin (not collagen) transports O2, and collagen is structural. Insulin is a hormone that regulates blood glucose, antibodies (immunoglobulins) protect against infection, and actin and myosin contract muscle.

q: A mixture of the three amino acids in the table undergoes electrophoresis at pH 6.0. Which result is expected?
c: Lys moves to the − electrode, Asp to the + electrode, Gly stays
Lys moves to the + electrode, Asp to the − electrode, Gly stays
All three move to the − electrode, but at different speeds
Gly moves to the + electrode, while Lys and Asp stay in place
h: If pH < pI the amino acid is net positive; if pH > pI it is net negative; at pH = pI the net charge is zero.
w: At pH 6.0, lysine (pH below its pI) is net positive and moves to the negative electrode; aspartic acid (pH above its pI) is net negative and moves to the positive electrode; glycine is at its pI (zwitterion) and does not move.

q: Which biomolecule is correctly matched with the linkage that joins its building blocks?
h: Think of the condensation reaction that builds each polymer and the functional group it forms.
w: Amino acids are joined by amide (peptide) bonds. Fats use ester bonds, polysaccharides use glycosidic (acetal) bonds, and nucleic acids use phosphodiester bonds in their backbone.

q: Alanine, H<sub>2</sub>N–CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)–COOH, has a pI of 6.0. Which form is present mainly in a solution at pH 11?
h: At a pH well above the pI, OH<sup>−</sup> removes H<sup>+</sup>. Which groups lose a proton?
w: In basic solution both acidic groups are deprotonated: –COOH → –COO− and –NH+3 → –NH2, giving H2N–CH(CH3)–COO− (net −1). The zwitterion is the main form near the pI, not at pH 11.

q: Aspartic acid has the side chain –CH<sub>2</sub>COOH. What is its net charge in blood at physiological pH (7.4)?
h: At pH 7.4, every –COOH is ionized and the α-amino group is still –NH+3. Add up the charges.
w: At pH 7.4: α-COO− (−1), side-chain COO− (−1), α-NH+3 (+1). Net = −1, which is why Asp is called an acidic amino acid. Answering 0 forgets the ionized side chain.

q: A membrane protein has an α-helix that passes through the nonpolar interior of the lipid bilayer. Which side chains would most likely face the fatty acid tails?
h: “Like dissolves like”: which R groups are hydrocarbons with no charge or polar groups?
w: The lipid tails are nonpolar, so they contact nonpolar (hydrophobic) side chains such as Leu, Val and Ile. Basic, acidic and polar side chains prefer water and are found on surfaces exposed to the cytosol or the outside of the cell.

q: In a folded protein, which pair of side chains would most likely form a salt bridge?
h: A salt bridge is an ionic (electrostatic) attraction. Which pair carries opposite charges?
w: A salt bridge forms between a positively charged side chain (Lys) and a negatively charged one (Asp). Leu/Val form hydrophobic interactions, Ser/Thr form hydrogen bonds, and two Cys form a disulfide bond.

q: Carbon monoxide poisoning is dangerous mainly because CO
c: binds the iron in hemoglobin more tightly than O<sub>2</sub> does
hydrolyzes the peptide bonds in hemoglobin's four chains
oxidizes the heme iron and converts hemoglobin into myoglobin
denatures plasma albumin so blood can no longer carry CO<sub>2</sub>
h: Hemoglobin carries O<sub>2</sub> by binding it to the Fe<sup>2+</sup> in each heme group. What happens if another molecule takes that spot?
w: Hemoglobin in red blood cells transports O2 from the lungs to the tissues using Fe2+ in its heme groups. CO binds that iron far more tightly than O2, so less O2 is delivered. CO does not break peptide bonds.

q: Which amino acid side chain can form hydrogen bonds with water?
h: A hydrogen bond needs H bonded directly to F, O or N. Look for that in the side chain.
w: Serine has an O–H group in its side chain, so it can donate and accept hydrogen bonds with water (polar, hydrophilic). The other three side chains are only C and H, so they are nonpolar and hydrophobic.

q: Stomach acid (HCl, pH about 2) helps protein digestion. Which statement best describes how?
c: It denatures proteins, unfolding them so pepsin can reach the peptide bonds.
It hydrolyzes every peptide bond, releasing free amino acids.
It breaks the primary structure by oxidizing the side chains.
It converts proteins to glucose so they can be absorbed.
h: Low pH disrupts salt bridges and hydrogen bonds. Which levels of structure does that affect, and which bonds does pepsin hydrolyze?
w: HCl denatures proteins, disrupting secondary and tertiary structure so the chain unfolds and pepsin can hydrolyze the exposed peptide bonds. Acid alone does not break the primary structure into free amino acids; the enzymes do that.

q: The body makes nonessential amino acids by transferring an –NH<sub>2</sub> from glutamate to an α-keto acid. Why can't essential amino acids be made this way?
c: The body cannot make the α-keto acid carbon skeletons of essential amino acids.
There is not enough glutamate in cells to donate amino groups.
Essential amino acids contain no amino group.
Transamination works only in the stomach, not in cells.
h: Transamination needs two partners: an amino group donor and an α-keto acid acceptor. Which one is missing?
w: Transamination puts an –NH2 onto an α-keto acid. The body can make the keto acids (such as pyruvate → alanine) for nonessential amino acids but cannot synthesize the carbon skeletons of essential ones, so they must come from the diet. Amino groups (from glutamate) are not the limiting part.

q: A free lysine molecule, side chain –(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>4</sub>–NH<sub>2</sub>, is dissolved in blood plasma (pH 7.4). Adding up all its ionized groups gives what overall charge?
h: At pH 7.4, the α-carboxyl is –COO− and the α-amino is –NH+3. What happens to a basic side-chain amine?
w: –COO− (−1) + –NH+3 (+1) + side-chain –NH+3 (+1) = +1. Answering 0 forgets that the basic side chain is also protonated at physiological pH.

q: Of these four amino acids, only one is classified as basic, with a side chain that is protonated (+) in body fluids. Which one?
h: Basic side chains contain an extra amine-type nitrogen that can accept H<sup>+</sup>. An amide nitrogen is not basic.
w: Arginine's side chain (a guanidino group) is protonated and positive at pH 7.4. Glutamine contains N, but in an amide, which is neutral; aspartic acid is acidic and negative.

q: In the tertiary structure of an enzyme, the side chain of leucine lies next to the side chain of isoleucine in the protein's interior. Which interaction holds them together?
h: Classify both side chains: are they polar, charged, sulfur-containing or nonpolar hydrocarbons?
w: Leucine and isoleucine both have nonpolar hydrocarbon side chains, so they cluster together away from water by hydrophobic interactions. Salt bridges need opposite charges, and disulfide bonds need two cysteines.

q: In the tetrapeptide Met–Lys–Trp–Glu, which amino acid is at the C-terminal end, with a free –COO<sup>−</sup> group?
h: Peptides are written from the N-terminus (free –NH+3) on the left to the C-terminus on the right.
w: By convention, the N-terminal amino acid is written first (Met) and the C-terminal amino acid last, so Glu has the free carboxylate group.

q: A student links leucine, histidine and tyrosine into a three-residue chain, using each just once but in any order (for example, Leu–His–Tyr or Tyr–Leu–His). How many distinct sequences are possible?
h: Leu–His–Tyr and Tyr–His–Leu are different peptides because the N- and C-terminal ends differ. Count the possible orders.
w: There are 3 choices for the first position, 2 for the second and 1 for the last: 3 × 2 × 1 = 6. 27 (33) would allow repeats, which the problem does not.

q: Mercury and lead poisoning damage many enzymes. Heavy-metal ions such as Hg<sup>2+</sup> and Pb<sup>2+</sup> denature proteins mainly by
c: binding to cysteine –SH groups and breaking disulfide bonds
hydrolyzing the peptide bonds that join the amino acids
adding water across the C=O groups of the peptide backbone
forming new hydrogen bonds that tighten the α helix
h: Denaturation changes shape (secondary and higher), not the amino acid sequence. Which side chain is especially attracted to heavy metals?
w: Heavy-metal ions bind strongly to sulfur in –SH groups and to carboxylates, breaking disulfide bonds and salt bridges so the protein unfolds. Denaturation leaves the peptide bonds (primary structure) intact.

q: Red blood cells carry oxygen bound to hemoglobin. How does one hemoglobin molecule bind O<sub>2</sub>?
c: Each of its four heme groups holds an Fe<sup>2+</sup> ion that binds one O<sub>2</sub>.
Its single polypeptide chain binds one O<sub>2</sub> at a time.
It stores O<sub>2</sub> in muscle tissue rather than carrying it in blood.
Its iron must be Fe<sup>3+</sup> to bind O<sub>2</sub>.
h: Hemoglobin has four subunits, each with one heme. What metal ion and charge are in the heme?
w: Hemoglobin has four subunits, each with a heme whose Fe2+ binds one O2, so one hemoglobin carries up to four O2. Storing O2 in muscle is the job of myoglobin; Fe3+ (methemoglobin) cannot bind O2.

q: A biochemist treats a protein with a reducing agent that breaks all its disulfide bonds but no other bonds. Which level of structure is NOT changed?
c: the cross-links between cysteine side chains
h: The primary structure is the amino acid sequence held by peptide bonds. Are disulfide bonds part of that chain?
w: Disulfide bridges link side chains and help hold the tertiary (and sometimes quaternary) structure. The sequence of amino acids, held by peptide bonds, is untouched: the primary structure stays the same.

q: Corn protein is low in lysine, and bean protein is low in methionine. A vegetarian eats tortillas and beans at the same meal. Why is this a good choice?
c: Together they are complementary proteins supplying all essential amino acids.
Beans cause the body to synthesize the missing lysine from extra glucose.
Corn supplies nonessential amino acids, which then become essential ones.
Eating them together prevents the proteins from being hydrolyzed in digestion.
h: Essential amino acids cannot be made by the body. What happens when two foods are low in different essential amino acids?
w: Each food supplies the essential amino acid the other lacks, so together they are complementary proteins that provide all the essential amino acids. The body cannot make lysine (an essential amino acid) from glucose.

q: Using the molar masses in the table, what is the molar mass of the tripeptide Gly–Gly–Gly?
h: Each peptide bond forms by condensation, releasing one H<sub>2</sub>O. How many peptide bonds are in a tripeptide?
w: A tripeptide has 2 peptide bonds, so 2 H2O are lost: 3(75.07) − 2(18.02) = 225.21 − 36.04 = 189.17 g mol⁻¹. 225.21 forgets the water lost; 207.19 removes only one water; 243.23 adds a water instead of removing them.

q: Which amino acid contains sulfur AND can form a disulfide bridge with another molecule of the same amino acid?
h: A disulfide bridge, –S–S–, forms when two thiol (–SH) groups are oxidized.
w: Cysteine has a –CH2SH side chain, and two –SH groups oxidize to –S–S–. Methionine also contains sulfur, but as a thioether (–S–CH3) with no –SH, so it cannot form disulfides.

q: How is the side chain of the amino acid shown (as it exists at pH 7.4) classified?
h: Ignore the H3N+–CH–COO− backbone. Look only at the side chain: charged –COO−, charged –NH+3, –OH/–SH/amide, or only C and H?
w: The side chain is –CH2OH. The –OH can hydrogen bond with water but carries no charge, so serine is polar neutral.

q: How is the side chain of the amino acid shown (as it exists at pH 7.4) classified?
h: Ignore the H3N+–CH–COO− backbone. Look only at the side chain: charged –COO−, charged –NH+3, –OH/–SH/amide, or only C and H?
w: The side chain ends in a carboxylate (–COO−), which is negatively charged at pH 7.4, so aspartate is acidic. The backbone COO− does not count; every amino acid has one.

q: How is the side chain of the amino acid shown (as it exists at pH 7.4) classified?
h: Ignore the H3N+–CH–COO− backbone. Look only at the side chain: charged –COO−, charged –NH+3, –OH/–SH/amide, or only C and H?
w: The side chain ends in an –NH+3 group, positively charged at pH 7.4, so lysine is basic. The backbone H3N+ is on every amino acid.

q: Phenylalanine must be limited in the diet of people with PKU. How is the side chain of the amino acid shown (as it exists at pH 7.4) classified?
h: Ignore the H3N+–CH–COO− backbone. Look only at the side chain: charged –COO−, charged –NH+3, –OH/–SH/amide, or only C and H?
w: The side chain is a benzyl group (–CH2–C6H5) of only C and H, so phenylalanine is nonpolar and tends to be buried inside folded proteins.

q: How is the side chain of the amino acid shown (as it exists at pH 7.4) classified?
h: Ignore the H3N+–CH–COO− backbone. Look only at the side chain: charged –COO−, charged –NH+3, –OH/–SH/amide, or only C and H?
w: The side chain ends in an amide (–CONH2). Amides are polar but neither acidic nor basic at pH 7.4, so glutamine is polar neutral. Students often confuse it with glutamate, whose –COO− side chain is acidic.

q: Which amino acid has a nonpolar side chain?
h: A nonpolar side chain contains only carbon and hydrogen.
w: The correct structure is valine: its side chain is an isopropyl group, –CH(CH3)2, only C and H, so it is nonpolar. Serine (–CH2OH) is polar neutral, aspartate (–COO−) acidic and lysine (–NH+3) basic.

q: The dipeptide Ala–Gly is shown. The peptide bond joins which two labeled atoms?
h: A peptide bond is an amide bond: the carbonyl carbon of one amino acid bonded to the nitrogen of the next.
w: The peptide (amide) bond links the C=O carbon of alanine (b) to the N–H nitrogen of glycine (c). Atoms a and d are the α-carbons; the a–b and c–d bonds are ordinary C–C and N–C bonds inside each residue.

q: The –COOH group of glycine (first structure) reacts with the –NH<sub>2</sub> group of alanine (second structure), releasing H<sub>2</sub>O. Which product forms?
h: A peptide bond is an amide: C(=O)–NH. Glycine's carboxyl carbon bonds to alanine's nitrogen.
w: Condensation joins glycine's C=O carbon to alanine's N, giving the amide (peptide) bond of Gly–Ala; the free –NH2 stays on glycine and the free –COOH on alanine. The reversed dipeptide is Ala–Gly; the C(=O)–O–C(=O) structure is an anhydride, and the N–CH2 link has no C=O, so it is an amine, not an amide.

q: Which structure shows alanine as it mainly exists in blood plasma (pH 7.4)?
h: At pH 7.4 the carboxyl group has lost H<sup>+</sup> and the amino group has gained H<sup>+</sup>.
w: At physiological pH alanine is a zwitterion: –NH+3 and –COO−, net charge 0. The uncharged form is not actually present in water; –NH+3/–COOH is the low-pH form, and –NH2/–COO− is the high-pH form.

q: Glycine is dissolved in stomach acid at pH 1. Which structure is the main form present?
h: At very low pH, there is a lot of H<sup>+</sup>: every basic group is protonated and every acidic group keeps its H.
w: In strong acid both groups carry H: –NH+3 and –COOH, net charge +1. The zwitterion (net 0) dominates near pH 6, and –NH2/–COO− (net −1) at high pH.

q: Lysine is shown in its uncharged form. What is its net charge at pH 1?
h: At pH 1, protonate every amino group and leave the carboxyl group as –COOH.
w: At pH 1 both –NH2 groups (backbone and side chain) gain H+ to become –NH+3, and the –COOH stays neutral: net charge +2. Answering +1 forgets the side-chain amino group.

q: Aspartic acid is shown in its uncharged form. What is its net charge at pH 12?
h: At high pH every –COOH loses H+ and every –NH+3 loses H+ (becomes neutral –NH2).
w: At pH 12 both carboxyl groups become –COO− and the amino group is neutral –NH2: net charge −2. Answering −1 forgets the side-chain carboxyl.

q: Hair proteins (keratin) are held in shape by disulfide bridges, –S–S–. Which amino acid forms them?
h: A disulfide forms when two thiol (–SH) groups are oxidized and join.
w: The correct structure is cysteine: its side chain ends in a thiol, –SH. Oxidizing two cysteine –SH groups forms an –S–S– bridge (tertiary structure). Methionine has sulfur but as a thioether (–S–CH3) with no S–H; serine and threonine have –OH.

q: Four amino acids are drawn as they exist at pH 7.4. Which one is most likely found buried in the interior of a water-soluble, globular protein?
h: Ignore the common backbone. Look at each side chain: is it hydrocarbon only, or does it carry –OH, a charge, or N/O that attracts water?
w: Structure I is valine: its side chain, –CH(CH3)2, is pure hydrocarbon (nonpolar, hydrophobic), so it avoids water and is tucked inside the folded protein. II (threonine, –OH), III (glutamate, –COO−) and IV (arginine, charged guanidinium) are polar or charged and stay on the water-exposed surface.

q: Four amino acids are drawn at pH 7.4. Which one can link to another copy of itself through a disulfide bond in a protein?
h: A disulfide bond forms when two –SH groups are oxidized. Two structures contain sulfur; only one has an –SH.
w: Structure II is cysteine, whose side chain ends in a thiol (–SH). Two cysteine –SH groups are oxidized to a –S–S– disulfide bridge, which stabilizes tertiary structure. Structure IV (methionine) also contains sulfur, but as a thioether (–S–CH3) that cannot form a disulfide; I (serine) and III (threonine) have –OH groups.

q: The pK<sub>a</sub> values of the ionizable groups of glutamic acid are listed. What is its net charge at pH 7.0?
h: A group is deprotonated when the pH is above its pK<sub>a</sub>. Decide the charge on each group at pH 7, then add them up.
w: At pH 7.0 both carboxyl groups (pKa 2.2 and 4.3) are deprotonated to –COO− (−1 each) and the amino group (pKa 9.7) is still –NH+3 (+1): −1 − 1 + 1 = −1. "0" treats glutamate like a neutral amino acid and forgets the acidic side chain; −2 forgets the positive amino group.

q: Use the pK<sub>a</sub> table for glutamic acid. At approximately what pH is its net charge zero (its isoelectric point, pI)?
h: The zwitterion (net 0) exists between the two pK<sub>a</sub> values that bracket it. Which two? Average them.
w: Going up in pH, the charge goes +1 → 0 → −1 → −2 at pKa 2.2, 4.3 and 9.7. The net-zero form lies between pKa 2.2 and 4.3, so pI ≈ (2.2 + 4.3)/2 = 3.3. Averaging 2.2 and 9.7 (6.0) is the formula for an amino acid with a neutral side chain, which does not apply here.

q: The dipeptide shown is drawn as it exists at pH 7.4. What is its name, written from the N-terminal end?
h: The N-terminus is the residue with the free –NH+3. Identify each side chain: –CH2OH is serine, –CH3 is alanine.
w: The residue with the free –NH+3 has a –CH2OH side chain: serine is the N-terminal residue. The residue with the free –COO− has a –CH3 side chain: alanine. Written N → C, the dipeptide is Ser–Ala. "Ala–Ser" reads the structure from the wrong end; threonine would need a –CH(OH)CH3 side chain.

q: Which structure is a dipeptide, two amino acids joined by a peptide bond?
h: A peptide bond is an amide: the –COOH of one amino acid joined to the α-amino group of another. Check each structure for two α-carbons and an amide between them.
w: Structure I has two α-carbons (each with its own N) connected through a –C(=O)–NH– amide: it is the dipeptide Gly–Ala. II (asparagine) contains an amide, but in its side chain; it is a single amino acid. III joins glycine to serine through an ester (–C(=O)–O–), not a peptide bond. IV (lysine) has two amino groups but no amide at all.

q: The table lists denaturing treatments and the interactions each one disrupts. Which level of protein structure survives every treatment in the table?
h: Which level is held together by covalent peptide bonds? None of the listed treatments is hydrolysis.
w: Every interaction in the table (hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions, salt bridges, disulfide bonds) is part of the secondary, tertiary or quaternary structure. None of the treatments breaks the peptide bonds, so the primary structure (the amino acid sequence) survives denaturation. Only hydrolysis (digestion) breaks primary structure.

q: Two regular folding patterns of a polypeptide backbone are compared in the table. Which identification is correct?
c: I = α-helix, II = β-pleated sheet; both are secondary structure
I = β-pleated sheet, II = α-helix; both are secondary structure
I = α-helix, II = β-pleated sheet; both are tertiary structure
h: The coil is the helix; the side-by-side strands are the sheet. Both are backbone hydrogen-bond patterns, so they belong to the same structural level.
w: A coiled spiral with hydrogen bonds along one chain is the α-helix (I); strands lying side by side held by hydrogen bonds between them form the β-pleated sheet (II). Both are stabilized by backbone C=O···H–N hydrogen bonds, so both are secondary structure. Tertiary structure involves side-chain interactions, not the backbone pattern.

head: Feature
I
II
rows: zig-zag strands lying side by side
within one chain, between C=O and N–H four residues apart

q: The curve shows the titration of fully protonated glycine (H<sub>3</sub>N<sup>+</sup>–CH<sub>2</sub>–COOH) with NaOH. At which labeled point does the zwitterion, with a net charge of zero, predominate?
h: The first equivalent of OH− removes the –COOH proton; the second removes the –NH+3 proton. Where is exactly one proton gone?
w: After exactly one equivalent of base (point b, pH ≈ 6) the carboxyl group has lost its proton (–COO−) but the amino group is still –NH+3: the zwitterion, net charge 0. At a (pH = pKa1 = 2.3) half the molecules are still the +1 cation; at c (pH = pKa2 = 9.6) half have become the −1 anion; at d the anion dominates.

q: The titration curve of fully protonated glycine with NaOH is shown. What is the isoelectric point (pI) of glycine?
h: The pI is the pH where the net charge is zero: midway between the two pK<sub>a</sub> values, which are the pH values at the two half-equivalence points (a and c).
w: The flat regions give pKa1 ≈ 2.3 (point a) and pKa2 ≈ 9.6 (point c). The zwitterion dominates between them, at the steep rise after one equivalent (point b): pI = (2.3 + 9.6)/2 ≈ 6.0. 2.3 and 9.6 are the individual pKa values, not the pI; 7.0 is neutral water, which has nothing to do with the amino acid.

q: Curve 1 is the normal oxygen-binding curve of hemoglobin in blood at pH 7.4. Curve 2 was measured in a blood sample from an actively exercising muscle. Which condition explains the shift?
c: Higher CO<sub>2</sub> and lower pH, which make hemoglobin release O<sub>2</sub> more easily
Lower CO<sub>2</sub> and higher pH, which make hemoglobin bind O<sub>2</sub> more tightly
Carbon monoxide in the sample, which blocks the O<sub>2</sub>-binding sites
A higher O<sub>2</sub> pressure in the lungs, which saturates hemoglobin
h: Curve 2 needs a higher O<sub>2</sub> pressure to reach the same % saturation: lower affinity. What does working muscle add to the blood?
w: Curve 2 lies to the right: at any O2 pressure hemoglobin is less saturated, meaning it holds O2 less tightly and unloads it more readily. Working muscle produces CO2 and H+ (lower pH), which bind hemoglobin and reduce its O2 affinity (the Bohr effect): more O2 is delivered where it is needed. Higher pH would shift the curve left.

q: Use the oxygen-binding curve of hemoglobin. Blood leaves the lungs at an O<sub>2</sub> pressure of 100 mmHg and reaches resting tissue where the O<sub>2</sub> pressure is 40 mmHg. About what percentage of the hemoglobin's O<sub>2</sub>-binding sites unload their O<sub>2</sub> in the tissue?
h: Read the % saturation at 100 mmHg and at 40 mmHg from the curve. The difference is what was delivered.
w: From the curve, saturation is about 98% at 100 mmHg (lungs) and about 77% at 40 mmHg (tissue). The difference, roughly 98 − 77 ≈ 20%, is the fraction of sites that released O2. "75%" is the saturation remaining in the tissue, not the amount unloaded; the sigmoid shape means most of the O2 stays bound until the pressure falls further, as in exercising muscle.

q: Which of the structures drawn is an amino acid of the kind found in proteins?
h: A protein amino acid has an amino group AND a carboxylic acid group attached to the same (alpha) carbon.
w: Structure A is alanine: an –NH<sub>2</sub> and a –COOH are both bonded to the same carbon, the α carbon, which also carries the side chain –CH<sub>3</sub>. Lactic acid has –OH and –COOH (a hydroxy acid, no nitrogen); 2-aminoethanol has an amine and an alcohol but no carboxyl group; propanamide contains an amide group but no free amine or carboxylic acid.

q: Two side chains lie next to each other in the tertiary structure of an enzyme. For which pair is hydrogen bonding the main attraction holding them together?
h: Hydrogen bonds need an O–H or N–H plus an O or N. Charged pairs make salt bridges; hydrocarbon pairs are hydrophobic; two –SH groups make a disulfide.
w: Both serine and threonine side chains have an –OH, so one O–H can hydrogen-bond to the oxygen of the other: hydrogen bonding. Leucine/valine are hydrocarbons (hydrophobic interaction), lysine/glutamate carry opposite charges (salt bridge), and two cysteines are joined by a covalent disulfide bond.

q: A chemist adjusts an alanine solution to pH 12 with NaOH. Which of the structures drawn is the predominant form of alanine at this pH?
h: At high pH, OH− removes every acidic proton: the –COOH loses H+, and so does the –NH+3.
w: At pH 12 the carboxyl group is deprotonated (–COO−) and the base has also pulled the proton off the –NH+3, leaving a neutral –NH2: the anion H2N–CH(CH3)–COO−, net charge −1. The zwitterion is the pH 7 form, the cation the pH 1 form; the fully uncharged –NH2/–COOH molecule is not the major form at any pH.

q: The tripeptide drawn (uncharged form) is completely hydrolyzed by digestive enzymes. What are the products?
c: Glycine, alanine and serine, using 2 H<sub>2</sub>O
Glycine, alanine and serine, using 3 H<sub>2</sub>O
One amino acid and one dipeptide, using 1 H<sub>2</sub>O
Three different carboxylic acids and NH<sub>3</sub>
h: Count the peptide (amide) bonds: each one hydrolyzed consumes one water and separates two amino acids.
w: A tripeptide has two peptide bonds, so complete hydrolysis uses 2 H2O and releases the three free amino acids: glycine (H side chain), alanine (–CH3) and serine (–CH2OH). "3 H2O" counts amino acids instead of bonds. Hydrolysis breaks only the amide bonds; the α-amino groups stay on their amino acids as NH+3, not as free NH3.

q: A water-soluble enzyme is placed in a nonpolar solvent such as hexane. Which change in its structure is most likely, and why does activity fall?
c: Hydrophobic side chains turn outward and polar ones inward, so the tertiary structure and active site are lost
The peptide bonds hydrolyze, so the primary structure and with it the active site are destroyed
New disulfide bonds form between all of the cysteine residues, locking the active site shut
The α-helices convert into β-sheets, but the shape of the active site itself is unchanged
h: In water, hydrophobic R groups hide inside and polar R groups face out. What happens when the solvent itself is nonpolar?
w: In hexane the driving force reverses: hydrophobic side chains are now happiest facing the solvent and polar side chains cluster inside, so the protein refolds or unfolds and the precisely shaped active site is lost: denaturation of tertiary structure. The covalent peptide bonds are not broken by a solvent (that needs hydrolysis), and disulfide formation requires an oxidizing agent.
